\chapter{Asking}
\label{ch:zh-asking}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand, say, read and write \zh{吗}, \zh{你好吗}, \zh{是吗} and \zh{好不好}, turn any statement I already own into a yes-or-no question by either of Mandarin's two patterns, and score listening, speaking, reading and writing separately.}

Before this chapter the track could greet, name, count to five and say what it read, and could not ask a yes-or-no question about any of it. One character closes that and does more than its own weight: \zh{吗} goes on the end of a finished sentence and changes nothing else, so every statement already taught becomes a question. The second pattern costs no character at all -- it is \zh{不}, held since the negation lesson, placed between two copies of a word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ma]{Hear \emph{ma} — the syllable that asks}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-hear-ma}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{look}, \textbf{book}, and \textbf{read a book} in Mandarin. Name your four scores from the looking-and-reading payoff, and which of the four was lowest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ma} — \textbf{the question particle}
\end{quote}

Say it light, short and flat. It carries \textbf{no tone}, which makes it the first syllable in this book with none — every earlier one has been first, second, third or fourth. Give it none at all, and no stress either.

It also carries \textbf{no meaning} on its own. There is nothing to translate. What it does is turn the sentence in front of it into a question, and it does that without moving a single other word.

Hear \emph{kàn shū} and then \emph{kàn shū ma}. The words are identical and in the same order; only the light syllable at the end is new, and only the second one is asking.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\zh{吗} — the mouth, then the horse}

\label{lesson:ZH-W19-ma-observe}



\begin{quote}
Say the neutral question syllable. Then write \zh{口} in three strokes, and write \zh{书} once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
Write \textbf{\zh{吗}} in six strokes, left part first and complete:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{口}} on the left, small and lifted toward the top: the left vertical, then the horizontal that turns down the right side without lifting, then the closing bottom bar. Three strokes, as you already write it.
  \item \textbf{\zh{马}} on the right, which supplies only the sound: a horizontal that turns down, then a long stroke that turns twice and hooks, then one wide horizontal across the whole right side. Three strokes.
\end{itemize}

Six strokes, five lifts. The \textbf{\zh{口}} shrinks to about a third of the square and sits high; the wide final horizontal is the widest thing in the character and runs almost to the right edge.

The left half is doing real work even though it is not saying anything: \textbf{\zh{口}} means \emph{mouth}, and it marks \zh{吗} as one of a family of characters that exist only to be spoken.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\zh{吗}} once. Say \textbf{mouth, mouth, mouth — turn, turn-and-hook, long bar}. Finish the whole \zh{口} before starting the right half, and keep it small.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%90\%97.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{吗}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\zh{吗} — copy it, and keep the mouth small}

\label{lesson:ZH-W19-ma-guided}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\zh{看书}} and give its meaning. Then air-write \textbf{mouth, mouth, mouth — turn, turn-and-hook, long bar}. Say \textbf{see} and \textbf{primary school}, and write \textbf{\zh{看见}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{吗}} twice beside the model. On the second copy, stop after the third stroke and check two things before going on: the \zh{口} fills about a third of the width, and its bottom sits above the middle of the square.

\subsection*{Your turn — Spaced Return}
Hear \textbf{read a book} and write \zh{看书} once without a model.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\zh{吗} — wait, then write the bar}

\label{lesson:ZH-W19-ma-delayed}



\begin{quote}
Say the neutral question syllable, then write \zh{书} once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\zh{吗}} for five seconds. Cover it, wait five more, then write it once. Uncover and check the order: all three strokes of \zh{口} before anything on the right.

Most characters give you a meaning to hang the shape on. This one does not — it means nothing by itself — so the route is all you have, and that is why it gets its own delay.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%90\%97.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{吗}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\zh{吗} — the sound meets the shape}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-ma}



\begin{quote}
Say the neutral question syllable. Then say \textbf{look} and \textbf{read a book}. Say \textbf{good-looking} and \textbf{primary-school pupil}, write \zh{小}, and recall your four looking-and-reading scores.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{吗}} — \emph{ma} — \textbf{the question particle}
\end{quote}

Hide the pinyin. Read \zh{吗}, give it no tone at all, and say what it does rather than what it means.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — one character, every statement}]
Put \textbf{\zh{吗}} at the \textbf{end} of a statement and the statement becomes a yes-or-no question. Nothing else changes:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{你看书}} — \emph{nǐ kàn shū} — you read books.
  \item \textbf{\zh{你看书吗}} — \emph{nǐ kàn shū ma} — \textbf{do} you read books?
\end{itemize}

Same words. Same order. One character added at the end.

That is worth stopping on, because it is not how English works: English moves words about and borrows a helper verb — \emph{you read} becomes \emph{do you read} — and Mandarin does neither. Every statement you can already make is now also a question you can ask, and there are no new words to learn to ask any of them.

Chinese closes both of those lines with a mark of its own — a small hollow circle for the statement and a question mark for the question. Neither mark is taught yet, so neither is printed here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear \emph{ma}. Wait three seconds, then write \textbf{\zh{吗}} once without a model. Then take any sentence you own and put \zh{吗} on the end of it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǐ hǎo ma]{Hear \emph{nǐ hǎo ma} — how are you}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-hear-nihaoma}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{hello}. Then say the neutral syllable that turns a statement into a question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{nǐ hǎo ma} — \textbf{how are you?}
\end{quote}

The very first thing this book taught you, with the very newest thing on the end of it. No new word arrives here at all.

Two third tones in a row still slide the first one up, exactly as they do in \emph{nǐ hǎo} on its own — the light \emph{ma} on the end changes nothing about that.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǐ hǎo ma]{\zh{你好吗} — the greeting, asked}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-nihaoma}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{how are you}. Then write \zh{你} and \zh{好}. Write \textbf{\zh{好看}} too, and say what the \zh{好} is doing in it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{你好吗}} — \emph{nǐ hǎo ma} — \textbf{how are you?}
\end{quote}

Read the three known shapes from left to right: \zh{你}, \zh{好}, and the new \zh{吗} on the end. Every one of them is a character you have already written.

That is the whole of what \zh{吗} buys you. The book has been able to write \zh{你好} since its first page and has never once been able to ask anything. One character, six strokes, and the greeting turns into a question.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{你好吗}} once. Keep the three characters the same size — \zh{吗} is not smaller just because it means nothing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Retrieval 1 — greeting, or question?}

\label{lesson:ZH-R19-ma-two-r1}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{hello}, then \textbf{how are you}, and name the difference between them. Then say \textbf{book}, and recall your four scores from the primary-school payoff.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear the two meanings in mixed order. Say each Mandarin answer, read its unpointed card, then write it. Look at the last character before deciding whether you were greeted or asked.

\section[shì ma]{Hear \emph{shì ma} — is that so?}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-hear-shima}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{to be}, then say \textbf{how are you}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{shì ma} — \textbf{is that so? really?}
\end{quote}

Two syllables: the verb \textbf{to be}, falling hard, then the light question syllable. Nothing else.

This is the move you make when somebody tells you something and you want to show you heard it and to invite them to go on. English spends a whole phrase on it — \emph{is that so}, \emph{really}, \emph{oh yes?} — and Mandarin spends two syllables, one of which you learned yesterday.

Say it with the voice going \textbf{down} on \emph{shì} and staying light on \emph{ma}. Said flat it checks a fact; said with the fall exaggerated it registers surprise.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shì ma]{\zh{是吗} — checking what you were told}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-shima}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{is that so}. Then write \zh{是}, finishing \zh{日} before the lower body. Write \zh{书} and \zh{中} as well.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{是吗}} — \emph{shì ma} — \textbf{is that so? really?}
\end{quote}

Two known shapes, in the order you hear them: the nine-stroke \zh{是}, then the six-stroke \zh{吗}.

It is the shortest sentence in the book and it is a complete turn in a conversation. Somebody says something; you say \zh{是吗}; they keep going. Nothing about it is a fixed phrase to memorise — it is the yes-or-no rule applied to a one-word sentence.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{是吗}} once. Leave a clear boundary between the two characters, and keep \zh{是} the wider of the pair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hǎo bu hǎo]{Hear \emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — the question with the answer inside it}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-hear-haobuhao}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{good}, say \textbf{not}, and say \textbf{is that so}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{is it good? all right?}
\end{quote}

Three syllables and no new word in any of them: \textbf{good}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{good}.

This is Mandarin's \textbf{second} way of asking a yes-or-no question, and it is completely unlike the first. Where \emph{ma} adds a syllable that means nothing, this one says the word, then denies it, then says it again — and hands the listener both possible answers so they can pick one.

The \textbf{bu} in the middle goes light and toneless when it is caught between two copies of the same word. Say \emph{hǎo-bu-hǎo} with the stress on the first and last and the middle syllable almost swallowed.

Both questions ask the same thing. \emph{ma} is the neutral one; this one presses a little harder for a decision, which is why it is the one you hear at the end of a suggestion.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hǎo bu hǎo]{\zh{好不好} — the question that needed no new character}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-haobuhao}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{is it good}. Then write \zh{好} and \zh{不}, keeping all four strokes of \zh{不} separate. Say \textbf{secondary school}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — say it, deny it, say it again}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{好不好}} — \emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{is it good? all right?}
\end{quote}

Three known shapes, and the pattern behind them works on anything:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{是不是}} — \emph{shì bu shì} — is it, or isn't it?
  \item \textbf{\zh{看不看}} — \emph{kàn bu kàn} — will you look, or won't you?
\end{itemize}

Take any word that can be denied, put \textbf{\zh{不}} in the middle, and repeat it. That is the whole rule, and it needs no new character because you have had \zh{不} since the negation lesson.

Mandarin now gives you \textbf{two} ways to ask a yes-or-no question, and this book has just handed you both in one chapter:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{看书吗}} — the light syllable on the end
  \item \textbf{\zh{看不看书}} — the word, denied, and said again
\end{itemize}

They mean the same thing. Neither moves a word, and neither borrows a helper verb the way English does.

Both would be written with a question mark of Chinese's own at the end. That mark is not taught yet, so it is left off here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{好不好}} once. Then build one more of your own: take a word you can write, put \zh{不} in the middle, and write it again.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Retrieval 2 — which question was that?}

\label{lesson:ZH-R19-ma-three-r2}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{how are you}, \textbf{is that so}, and \textbf{is it good}, in that order. Then say \textbf{read a book} and write \textbf{\zh{中学}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear the three meanings in mixed order. Say each Mandarin answer, read its unpointed card, then write it. Before you write, decide which of the two question patterns it uses — the light syllable on the end, or the word denied in the middle.

\section[Practice]{Listening score — catch the question}

\label{lesson:ZH-R19-listening-three}



\begin{quote}
Say the light syllable that turns a statement into a question, and say where it goes. Then read \textbf{\zh{看书}} and \textbf{\zh{看见}} aloud.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
No cards and no writing. Hear each of the three, six times over in mixed order, and say the English meaning aloud before the next one starts.

Score listening on its own. A miss here is not a reading miss and not a writing miss, and it is repaired by hearing the item again rather than by looking at it.

The light \emph{ma} is the thing most often missed, because it is short, toneless and last. If you lose one, that is almost certainly the one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Reading score — no pinyin on the card}

\label{lesson:ZH-R19-reading-three}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{吗} once from memory, then \zh{是}. Then say \textbf{secondary-school pupil}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the three cards cold. No pinyin is printed on any of them. For each one, say it aloud and then give the English.

Score reading on its own. Reading and hearing fail differently here: by ear the light \emph{ma} is easy to lose, and on the page it is the most visible thing in the sentence because it is a whole character. The one you miss reading is more likely to be \zh{好不好}, where nothing is added and the clue is a repetition.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — the book can ask}

\label{lesson:ZH-C19-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{hello}, \textbf{to be}, \textbf{good}, \textbf{not}, and the light question syllable. Then write \textbf{\zh{中学生}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Four passes over the same four items, scored separately:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Listening.} Hear each of the four and give its English.
  \item \textbf{Speaking.} Be given the English and say the Mandarin, tones and all.
  \item \textbf{Reading.} Read four unpointed cards cold and give their meanings.
  \item \textbf{Writing.} Hear each one and write it with no model.
\end{itemize}

Record four numbers, not one. A reader who hears all four and writes none has a writing problem, and averaging the two hides it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Before this chapter the book had no way to ask a yes-or-no question at all. It could greet, name, count to five, say what it saw and say what it read, and it could not ask about any of it.

One character closed that, and it did more than its own weight: every statement this book has taught you is now also a question, because \zh{吗} goes on the end of a finished sentence and changes nothing else. The second pattern, \zh{好不好}, needed no new character whatsoever — it is \zh{不}, which you have had for chapters, put between two copies of a word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary}.
\end{tcolorbox}
